# From One Predictor to Many

For independent units $i=1,\ldots,n$, multiple linear regression models the
conditional mean of a continuous response using $p$ predictors:

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1X_{i1}+\cdots+\beta_pX_{ip}+\varepsilon_i,
\qquad
\operatorname{E}(\varepsilon_i\mid X_i)=0.
$$

The model is **linear in the unknown coefficients**. Predictors themselves may be
transformed, represented by indicators, or combined through prespecified
interactions while the model remains linear in $\boldsymbol\beta$.

In matrix form,

$$
\mathbf Y=\mathbf X\boldsymbol\beta+\boldsymbol\varepsilon,
$$

where the first column of $\mathbf X$ is usually all ones. The target
$\boldsymbol\beta$ is a population parameter under a specified model;
$\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}$ is an estimator before observing data and a numerical
estimate afterward.

# What a Coefficient Means

Holding the other modeled predictors fixed,

$$
\beta_j=
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_j}
\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X_1=x_1,\ldots,X_p=x_p)
$$

when the mean is linear and $X_j$ is continuous. Thus $\beta_j$ is the difference
in conditional mean per one-unit change in $X_j$, at common values of the other
predictors. For a binary indicator, it is the adjusted mean contrast between the
two encoded groups.

"Holding fixed" is a mathematical comparison, not necessarily a feasible
intervention. If two covariates cannot vary independently in the target
population, the coefficient may depend heavily on extrapolation. If a predictor
is a confounder, adjustment may reduce bias; if it is a mediator or collider,
adjustment may instead change or bias the target. Predictor selection must follow
the scientific question and data-generating process, not an automated p-value
search.

Without interaction terms, the model asserts that the slope for $X_j$ is the same
at every modeled value of the other predictors. With an interaction
$\beta_{12}X_1X_2$,

$$
\frac{\partial}{\partial x_1}\operatorname{E}(Y\mid X)
=\beta_1+\beta_{12}x_2,
$$

so the main-effect coefficient $\beta_1$ is the slope when $X_2=0$. Centering can
make that reference value scientifically meaningful without changing fitted
values.

# Least Squares and Projection

OLS minimizes

$$
\operatorname{RSS}(\mathbf b)
=(\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\mathbf b)^\mathsf{T}
 (\mathbf Y-\mathbf X\mathbf b).
$$

Differentiation gives the normal equations

$$
\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf Y.
$$

If $\mathbf X$ has full column rank,

$$
\boxed{
\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}
=(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf Y
}.
$$

Geometrically, the fitted vector
$\hat{\mathbf Y}=\mathbf H\mathbf Y$ is the orthogonal projection of
$\mathbf Y$ onto the column space of $\mathbf X$, where

$$
\mathbf H=\mathbf X(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X)^{-1}\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}.
$$

The residual vector is orthogonal to every included design column:
$\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf e=\mathbf 0$. These sample identities do not prove
that omitted causes are unrelated to included predictors.

The Frisch--Waugh--Lovell result gives an especially useful interpretation.
Regress $X_j$ on the other predictors and retain its residuals; regress $Y$ on
those same predictors and retain its residuals. The slope between the two sets of
residuals equals $\hat\beta_j$. A coefficient therefore uses only the variation in
$X_j$ that is not linearly explained by the other design columns.

# Identification and Sampling Uncertainty

Full column rank is an identification condition. Exact linear dependence---for
example, an intercept plus indicators for every category---means that multiple
coefficient vectors produce the same fitted values. Near dependence makes
coefficients estimable but unstable.

Conditional on $\mathbf X$, if

$$
\operatorname{E}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)=\mathbf 0,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\boldsymbol\varepsilon\mid\mathbf X)=\sigma^2\mathbf I,
$$

then

$$
\operatorname{E}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
=\boldsymbol\beta,
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(\hat{\boldsymbol\beta}\mid\mathbf X)
=\sigma^2(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X)^{-1}.
$$

Estimate $\sigma^2$ by

$$
s^2=\frac{\operatorname{RSS}}{n-p-1}.
$$

The standard error of coefficient $j$ is the square root of the corresponding
diagonal element of
$s^2(\mathbf X^\mathsf{T}\mathbf X)^{-1}$. Conditional normal errors give exact
small-sample $t$ and $F$ reference distributions. Heteroskedasticity-consistent
standard errors relax constant variance but do not repair a wrong mean function,
dependence, confounding, or poor overlap.

# Omitted Variables and Changing Coefficients

Suppose the true mean includes $Z$,

$$
Y=\beta_0+\beta_1X+\gamma Z+\varepsilon,
$$

but $Z$ is omitted. In a population linear projection, the short-regression slope
is

$$
\tilde\beta_1
=\beta_1+\gamma\frac{\operatorname{Cov}(X,Z)}{\operatorname{Var}(X)}.
$$

Omitted-variable bias therefore needs both an association between $Z$ and the
outcome conditional on $X$ and an association between $Z$ and $X$. Adding a
variable can legitimately change a coefficient because it changes the conditional
comparison, not merely because the original model was "incorrect."

In causal work, the right adjustment set is determined by the causal structure.
In prediction, a variable may be useful without having a causal interpretation.
In descriptive work, both adjusted and unadjusted associations may answer useful
but different questions.

# Worked Bioinformatics Design

Consider an RNA-expression summary $Y_i$ for each of 60 independent patient
specimens. A prespecified model is

$$
Y_i=\beta_0+\beta_1\operatorname{Treatment}_i
 +\beta_2\operatorname{Age}_i
 +\beta_3\operatorname{BatchB}_i+\varepsilon_i.
$$

- $\beta_1$ compares adjusted mean expression between treatment groups at the
  same age and batch under the model.
- $\beta_2$ is the adjusted mean difference per year of age.
- $\beta_3$ describes a batch contrast; it is not a biological effect.

The experimental units are the 60 patients. Multiple lanes, reads, or technical
replicates improve measurement or help estimate technical variation but do not
turn the study into a larger patient sample. If treatment is completely
confounded with batch, the design matrix cannot distinguish $\beta_1$ from
$\beta_3$; no regression algorithm can recover information absent from the
design.

Statistically, an estimated treatment coefficient and interval summarize an
adjusted contrast on the chosen expression scale. Biologically, interpretation
also requires the gene's function, effect magnitude, normalization, tissue
composition, and whether the specimens represent the target population.

# Assumptions, Diagnostics, and Sensitivity

| Assumption or issue | Consequence | Assessment | Sensitivity or remedy |
|---|---|---|---|
| Correct conditional mean | Misspecification makes coefficients misleading averages | Residual plots, partial-residual plots, domain knowledge | Transformations, splines, interactions, alternative model |
| Independent units | Correlated errors invalidate ordinary SEs | Sampling hierarchy and time/order metadata | Cluster-robust inference, mixed model, generalized least squares |
| Zero conditional error mean | Omitted causes and selection can bias coefficients | Design reasoning, causal diagram, negative controls | Better design, justified adjustment, quantitative sensitivity analysis |
| Constant variance | Classical SEs may be wrong and OLS inefficient | Residual spread by fitted values and groups | Robust SEs or explicit variance model |
| Full rank and adequate overlap | Coefficients may be unidentified or unstable | Rank, condition indices, predictor distributions | Redesign, combine parameters, regularize for prediction, narrow target |
| No dominant observations | A few units can control estimates | Leverage, studentized residuals, Cook's distance, DFBETAs | Verify records and report deletion diagnostics transparently |
| Accurate variables | Measurement error can bias several coefficients | Validation data, reliability studies | Measurement-error model; calibration; replicate assays |

A useful diagnostic sequence is: verify design and units; inspect missingness and
overlap; visualize residuals; examine leverage and influence; compare conventional
and robust uncertainty; test scientifically plausible nonlinearities and
interactions; and report how conclusions change. Diagnostics should be tied to a
failure mechanism, not used as a ritual pass/fail checklist.

Variable selection after looking at the same outcome changes the sampling
behavior of coefficients and p-values. If selection is unavoidable, separate
exploration from confirmation, validate out of sample, and acknowledge
post-selection uncertainty.

# Connections and Take-home Messages

- [Simple linear regression](simple-linear-regression.qmd) develops the one-predictor
  case and basic prediction intervals.
- [Likelihood and log-likelihood](../statistical-inference/likelihood-and-log-likelihood.qmd)
  connects Gaussian regression to likelihood-based estimation.
- [Sensitivity analysis and robustness](../statistical-inference/sensitivity-analysis-and-robustness.qmd)
  provides a framework for checking dependence on assumptions.
- [Selection bias and winner's curse](../statistical-inference/selection-bias-and-winners-curse.qmd)
  explains why data-dependent reporting can inflate coefficients.

1. A multiple-regression coefficient is a conditional comparison given the other
   modeled predictors.
2. Least squares projects the response onto the design space; full column rank is
   required for unique coefficients.
3. Adjustment changes the estimand and can reduce, create, or leave bias depending
   on the data-generating structure.
4. Robust standard errors address variance misspecification, not confounding,
   dependence, lack of overlap, or an incorrect mean model.
5. In bioinformatics, independent biological specimens determine inferential
   replication; technical observations do not substitute for them.
